blocks.text: A linked structure turns a sequence into a network of ownership and observation relationships. Its correctness depends on more than the values printed by a forward traversal. Every node must remain reachable through the intended owner, every observer must point to a live node or no node, and removal must not leave a second path that silently reaches released storage.

blocks.text: HarborWorks uses this chapter’s lists as a laboratory for those relationships, not as an automatic replacement for vectors. First learn to draw the links and repair them. Then ask whether a node-based representation actually fits the workload. An operation advertised as constant-time may still require a preceding linear search to find its location.

blocks.text: Creation should finish before publication. push_front allocates a candidate node, assigns its payload, connects its next owner to the previous head, and finally publishes the candidate as the new head. If allocation fails before the old head is moved, the existing list remains intact. The integer payload avoids a throwing assignment complication; a generic payload would need a more careful construction design.

blocks.text: Destruction has its own traversal problem. Letting a very long chain of nested unique_ptr members recursively destroy itself can consume one stack frame per node. The worked destructor repeatedly extracts the next owner and releases the current node after its next link has been emptied. This makes cleanup iterative for the chain. The algorithmic cost remains linear, but the call-stack depth no longer grows with the list length.

reading.title: Guided lab — Validate operation sequences, not isolated calls
paragraphs: Add an exercise method that removes every occurrence of a requested integer. Start with [2,1,2,2,3,2]. After removing two, both traversals of the doubly linked version should describe [1,3], in opposite directions. After removing a missing value, the sequence should be unchanged. Explain when the owning-link cursor should remain at the same link rather than advance after deletion.

Build a small model using std::vector<int> or std::list<int>. Generate a deterministic sequence of push and erase operations, apply each to both representations, and compare after every operation. Restrict the value domain so duplicates are common. A final-state-only comparison can miss a transient corruption that happens to be overwritten later.

For a doubly linked diagnostic validator, check the predecessor relation at every forward step, remember the final visited node, and compare it with tail. Also verify that backward values reverse the forward sequence. Keep the validator outside a performance measurement: its additional full scans intentionally cost linear work per mutation.

Design an iterator interface on paper. State which insertions preserve an iterator, which erasures invalidate it, and whether an iterator to the erased node can be compared or incremented afterward. Do not assume that rules from std::list automatically apply to a custom type. An interface must promise only what its representation and implementation maintain.

Finally, compare two workloads. The first appends ten thousand readings and scans all of them repeatedly. The second repeatedly splices at already known positions while preserving unrelated node addresses. Explain why the same container need not be appropriate for both. Include lookup, allocation, output construction, and cleanup in the comparison.
